walkthroughs.body_html:
Organisms Respond to Changes — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Organisms Respond to Changes brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Organisms Respond to Changes.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the key structural difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
options: Sucrose is pushed into the phloem by turgor pressure from leaf cells.
Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotes do not.
Prokaryotes have no DNA — that's why they have no nucleus.
Prokaryotes are always smaller than 1 micrometre and have no cytoplasm.

mcqs.q: How is sucrose loaded into the phloem at a source?
options: Sucrose diffuses passively into the phloem because it is more concentrated outside.
By active transport (using ATP) via companion cells, against a concentration gradient.
Sucrose is pushed into the phloem by turgor pressure from leaf cells.
Prokaryotes are always smaller than 1 micrometre and have no cytoplasm.
Sucrose is pushed into the phloem by turgor pressure from leaf cells.
Each new DNA molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand.
DNA replication produces two identical fully new molecules with no original material.
One daughter molecule contains both original strands; the other contains both new strands.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Monomer”?
options: Joining of two molecules with loss of water and formation of a new chemical bond.
Covalent bond between two sugar molecules formed by condensation.
Small repeating subunit that forms polymers, e.g. amino acid, monosaccharide, nucleotide.
Bond between glycerol and a fatty acid in triglycerides, formed by condensation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Condensation reaction”?
options: Small repeating subunit that forms polymers, e.g. amino acid, monosaccharide, nucleotide.
Bond between glycerol and a fatty acid in triglycerides, formed by condensation.
Joining of two molecules with loss of water and formation of a new chemical bond.
Covalent bond between two sugar molecules formed by condensation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Hydrolysis”?
options: Small repeating subunit that forms polymers, e.g. amino acid, monosaccharide, nucleotide.
Bond between glycerol and a fatty acid in triglycerides, formed by condensation.
Large molecule formed from many monomers joined by condensation reactions.
Breaking of a bond by addition of water; reverse of condensation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Polymer”?
options: Covalent bond between two sugar molecules formed by condensation.
Small repeating subunit that forms polymers, e.g. amino acid, monosaccharide, nucleotide.
Bond between glycerol and a fatty acid in triglycerides, formed by condensation.
Large molecule formed from many monomers joined by condensation reactions.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Ester bond”?
options: Bond between glycerol and a fatty acid in triglycerides, formed by condensation.
Large molecule formed from many monomers joined by condensation reactions.
Joining of two molecules with loss of water and formation of a new chemical bond.
Breaking of a bond by addition of water; reverse of condensation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Glycosidic bond”?
options: Covalent bond between two sugar molecules formed by condensation.
Joining of two molecules with loss of water and formation of a new chemical bond.
Small repeating subunit that forms polymers, e.g. amino acid, monosaccharide, nucleotide.
Large molecule formed from many monomers joined by condensation reactions.
